content.summary: Welcome to the reading mission on mixed conditionals. In this module, you will read about how past actions and decisions affect our everyday lives right now. You will learn how to combine past perfect clauses with present consequence clauses to talk about alternative life paths.

linguisticTarget.grammar: If + past perfect, would/could/might + base verb for mixed conditional sentences.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Essential words for discussing life decisions, scholarships, regrets, and future opportunities.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts specifically for cause-and-effect relationships between past events and present situations.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about personal choices and life paths.
Locate specific details regarding past actions and their current results in a reading passage.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns involving mixed conditional sentences.

contextWarmup.prompt: Think about a major choice you made last year. How does it affect your daily life today?
options: It changes my daily schedule and career path completely.
It has no connection to what I do today.
It only affected my life for one single week.
contextWarmup.explanation: Major decisions usually create long-lasting changes in our routine and future direction, which is the exact idea behind mixed conditionals.

rules: Formula: If + past perfect, would/could/might + base verb. Example: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
The if-clause uses past perfect (had + past participle) to show an unreal past action or decision that did not happen.
The main clause uses would/could/might + base verb to show a present result or current state.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often mix up the time markers in conditional sentences by using present tenses in the if-clause when talking about past regrets.
commonTrap.wrong: If I study hard last year, I would pass the exam today.
commonTrap.correct: If I had studied hard last year, I would pass the exam today.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Mixed Conditionals
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice past conditions and present results:

complements.text: the scholarship, I would live in London now

items.exampleSentence: I regret not taking that opportunity when I had the chance.
She won a full scholarship to study at Cambridge University.
items.collocation: win a scholarship / apply for a scholarship

items.exampleSentence: Every decision has consequences that we must face later.
That business investment turned out to be very profitable.
He decided to pursue a career in software engineering.
items.collocation: pursue a career / pursue a dream

items.exampleSentence: I am grateful for all the support my family has given me.
This job offer is a great opportunity for career growth.
The current economic situation is quite challenging for everyone.
They have maintained a strong relationship for over ten years.
If I had practiced more, I would be fluent in Spanish now.

paragraphs: Tom sat at his desk in London, looking at an old photo album from his university days. He often thought about the choices he made five years ago. Back then, he received a scholarship to study architecture abroad, but he turned it down because he wanted to stay near his hometown. If he had accepted that scholarship, his entire career path would be completely different today. He might be working in a famous design firm in Europe right now.

Despite having moments of regret, Tom knows his current situation has many positive points. Because he stayed home, he built a strong relationship with his local business partners and started his own successful company. If he had moved away, he would not have these wonderful colleagues around him today. He feels grateful for his current life, even though he often wonders about what could have been.

content.summary: Practical guide on building mixed conditional sentences in English to connect past actions with present realities.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: The Past If-Clause
blueprintItems.example: If I had studied harder in university...

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: The Present Result Clause
blueprintItems.formula: subject + would / could / might + base verb
blueprintItems.example: ...I would have a better job now.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Combining Past Condition and Present Result
blueprintItems.formula: If + past perfect, would + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If she had saved her money, she could buy a car today.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after the if-clause when it comes at the beginning of the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If I had caught the train I would be at work now.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If I had caught the train, I would be at work now.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the dependent if-clause from the main independent clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use 'would have' in the if-clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If you would have told me, I would know the answer.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If you had told me, I would know the answer.
mechanicsRules.why: The if-clause in mixed conditionals requires the past perfect tense (had + V3), not modal verbs.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of every sentence and keep proper noun pronouns correct.
mechanicsRules.badExample: if i had lived in paris, i would speak French fluently.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If I had lived in Paris, I would speak French fluently.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences must start with capital letters, and languages like French are always capitalized.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform the statement into a mixed conditional sentence starting with 'If':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I didn't study French in school, so I don't speak it fluently now.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'If I had studied...' in the first clause.
targetAnswers: If I had studied French in school, I would speak it fluently now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Convert the past negative fact into a past perfect affirmative condition (If I had studied) and the present negative fact into a modal result (I would speak).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform the statement into a mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She didn't buy the house, so she rents an apartment today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use past perfect for buying and would/could for renting.
targetAnswers: If she had bought the house, she wouldn't rent an apartment today.
If she had bought the house, she would not rent an apartment today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The past action uses 'had bought', and the present situation changes to 'wouldn't rent an apartment today'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the correct verbs to complete the mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If he ________ (train) harder last month, he would be in the race today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the past perfect form of 'train'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Mixed conditionals require 'had' plus the past participle (had trained) in the if-clause to show a past action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the result clause of this mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If I had gone to bed early last night, I ________ (not feel) tired right now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present result clause uses 'would / wouldn't' followed by the base verb 'feel'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capitalization in the following mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if anna had taken the job she would live in paris now
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize names and places, and add a comma after the if-clause.
targetAnswers: If Anna had taken the job, she would live in Paris now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns like Anna and Paris require capital letters, and a comma must separate the if-clause from the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the grammar error in this mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If we would have saved money, we could buy a new car today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Remove 'would have' from the if-clause and use past perfect.
targetAnswers: If we had saved money, we could buy a new car today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Never use modal verbs like 'would have' in the if-clause. Use 'had' + past participle instead.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this sentence as a mixed conditional starting with 'If':
practicumQuestions.promptText: He missed his flight, so he is stuck at the airport this evening.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'had missed' or 'hadn't missed' depending on context.
targetAnswers: If he hadn't missed his flight, he wouldn't be stuck at the airport this evening.
If he had not missed his flight, he would not be stuck at the airport this evening.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A past mistake ('missed flight') connects to a present condition ('stuck at the airport').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete mixed conditional sentence based on this prompt: You didn't learn guitar when you were young. You cannot play in the band today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'If I had learned...' or 'If I had played...'
targetAnswers: If I had learned guitar when I was young, I could play in the band today.
If I had learned to play the guitar when I was younger, I could play in the band today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Connect the past lack of learning with the present inability to play in the band.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a mixed conditional sentence for this situation: She didn't accept the promotion last year. She is working in the same position today.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'had accepted' and 'wouldn't be working' or 'would have a better position'.
targetAnswers: If she had accepted the promotion last year, she wouldn't be working in the same position today.
If she had accepted the promotion last year, she would have a different job today.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A past career decision links directly to the current professional status.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Convert the following facts into a single mixed conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: They didn't wear warm jackets, so they are cold right now.
targetAnswers: If they had worn warm jackets, they wouldn't be cold right now.
If they had worn warm jackets, they would not be cold right now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Past action ('worn warm jackets') affects the present physical feeling ('cold right now').

content.summary: Mastering mixed conditionals requires careful attention to sentence rhythm, modal verb contractions, and stress placement. When you connect past choices with present realities, your voice needs to signal the shift from a hypothetical past event to a current consequence. Native speakers often reduce auxiliary verbs like 'had' to 'd' and 'would' to 'd', while keeping the main content words clear and prominent.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pausing slightly between the past condition clause and the present result clause. Use falling intonation at the end of the sentence to show certainty about the present outcome. Keep your articulation sharp on key vocabulary such as consequence, investment, and opportunity.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Contraction
pillars.explanation: In fast spoken English, 'If I had studied' becomes 'If I'd studied', and 'I would be' becomes 'I'd be'. Practice linking these sounds smoothly without pausing too long between words.

pillars.name: Clause Juncture
pillars.target: Natural pause between condition and result
pillars.explanation: When speaking mixed conditionals, insert a brief micro pause with your breath right after the comma separating the if clause from the main clause.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.target: Highlighting past actions and present states
pillars.explanation: Place primary sentence stress on the main verbs and adjectives that carry the core meaning, such as regret, fluent, and grateful.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress shifts slightly as the word form changes from verb to noun, but the middle syllable remains prominent.
The primary stress moves from the first syllable in the noun to the second syllable in the adjective.
Both words maintain stress on the third syllable, showing consistent secondary syllable patterns.
The stress moves from the first syllable of the adjective to the second syllable of the noun form.
